To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the approval process for a multicenter genetic epidemiological study differed widely across European countries and was often slow.
the ethics approval process in Europe is highly variable and that harmonisation of the approval process is required to improve efficiency and reduce delays in the approval process.
the approval processes for research ethics committees differed widely between countries in Europe.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ethical issues that may arise when conducting research on human subjects, particularly in a clinical setting.
the ethical and legal aspects of the use of genetic information in clinical practice and in research.
the ethics of the conduct of research in patients who lack capacity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GenOSept project demonstrated the feasibility of conducting an international genetic epidemiological study in sepsis.

there are significant differences in ethics approval procedures in European countries, which can have a substantial impact on the time taken to obtain ethics approval, and the number of centres participating in the study.
the ethics approval process is complex and challenging.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the European Clinical Trials regulation will not solve all problems.
the GenOSept study was successful in its aim to identify genetic factors that influence sepsis outcomes.

the GenOSept study was successful because the project team was committed to the project, the project was well funded, there was a strong scientific and clinical rationale for the project, and the investigators were able to adapt to the local requirements of the RECs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
harmonisation is urgently needed, not just in Europe, but also worldwide.
the ethics approval process for international studies is not a simple matter of submitting a protocol to a central REC.

harmonisation of REC processes across Europe is essential if we are to realise the benefits of the European Clinical Trials regulation and avoid unnecessary delays in the conduct of multicentre research.
